stories.headline: Sources: Maxx Crosby shut down Rams trade talks after failed Ravens deal
stories.summary: The Rams pursued Maxx Crosby shortly after his trade from the Raiders to the Ravens fell through, sources told NFL Network.
stories.body:
Before there was Myles, there was Maxx.

The Los Angeles Rams turned the NFL on its ear this spring with their blockbuster trade for Myles Garrett. But if the Rams had their initial wish, it would've been Maxx Crosby instead.

Sources told NFL Network that Los Angeles pursued Crosby shortly after his trade from the Las Vegas Raiders to the Baltimore Ravens fell through because of a failed physical.

Other teams were interested, but the Rams, with their propensity to swing big, were the strongest club pushing for a deal, according to sources.

But before there could be anything official, Crosby let it be known to anyone interested that he did not want to be traded. He wanted to remain with the Raiders, and he let his own organization know as well.

Crosby famously responded to the failed trade with: "I'm a Raider. I'm back. Run that (expletive)." The five-time Pro Bowler delivered a similar message to the Rams and other teams who wanted him.

Of course, the original plan was for the Raiders to trade Crosby to the Ravens in what was one of the biggest moves of the offseason, with two first-rounders heading back to Las Vegas. But with Baltimore not comfortable with Crosby's surgically repaired knee, the deal was off.

Sources say several teams came to the Raiders hoping to do a trade, but nothing even came remotely close because teams wanted "pennies on the dollars," in the words of one source.

In other words, those interested teams hoped Las Vegas was trying to dump Crosby for a cheap price, which was a non-starter.

Other teams such as the Eagles, Cowboys, and 49ers were monitoring and interested.

Yet no deal was coming, prompting the Rams to turn their attention to Garrett for their blockbuster this summer.

As for the Raiders team Crosby returned to, after they spent hundreds of millions in free agency, they were a much more talented team than when the Crosby trade to Baltimore was initially executed.

Once Crosby made clear he did not want to be traded again, it was over. As for Crosby's knee, sources say he's had no issues and is said to be in excellent health.

stories.headline: Premier League VAR review: Was Sunderland's penalty legit vs. Arsenal?
stories.summary: VAR often causes Premier League controversy, but how are decisions made and are they correct? Our resident ref, Andy Davies, explains all.
stories.body:
The video assistant referee causes controversy every week, whether it be the Premier League, Champions League or FA Cup, but how are those decisions made and are they correct?

For the 2026-27 season, we are taking a look at the major incidents to explain the process in terms of both VAR protocol and the laws of the game. The most surprising, controversial and complicated decisions will be examined all season long right here.

Andy Davies (@andydaviesref) is a former Select Group referee, with over 12 seasons on the elite list, working across the Premier League and Championship. With extensive experience at the elite level, he has operated within the VAR space in the Premier League and offers a unique insight into the processes, rationale and protocols that are delivered on a matchday.

Should Sunderland have been given a penalty vs. Arsenal?

Sunderland 0-2 Arsenal (Sept. 12)

Referee: John Brooks

VAR: Stuart Attwell

Time: 54 min

Incident: Penalty awarded to Sunderland

What happened: With the score 0-0 early in the second half, Arsenal were left frustrated as defender Ezri Konsa was adjudged to have fouled Sunderland's Dan Ballard after a Sunderland corner, and referee John Brooks pointed to the spot.

VAR decision: VAR checked and confirmed the on-field decision of a penalty kick to Sunderland.

VAR review: Brooks' live comms described Konsa's actions on Ballard as being "all over him at the near post, facing the wrong way." Having considered the communication from the referee, VAR ruled that he was accurate in his description and his rationale for awarding a penalty kick, and confirmed the decision as correct.

Verdict and insight: With the heightened profile, focus, and referees asked to be more assertive in set-play situations such as corners, there was a high chance that a small number of penalty kicks would be awarded incorrectly, and this was an example of it playing out in real-time.

From the referee's on-field position, this incident would have looked like Konsa was clumsy with his contact on Ballard. As both players fall to the ground, referee Brooks believed that it was the Arsenal player who was pulling, deliberately facing away from the ball and committing a holding offense -- the type of foul the football world was hoping would be penalized this season.

However, from the replays, it was clear that though Arsenal's Konsa engaged with Ballard with normal contact, Ballard using his left arm to pull Konsa's shirt made the Arsenal defender spin and land on the Sunderland center back. Any punishable offense was, in fact, committed by Ballard and the restart should have been a defensive free kick.

Mikel Arteta was fuming afterwards and it's difficult to understand why VAR did not intervene in this situation given the information available to him, as it was a clear but understandable on-field error by the referee -- the referee's live description of the incident did not match the replay pictures, and this should be a red flag to the VAR.

This was a poor non-intervention by VAR, and an on-field review should have been recommended.

Why was Forest's Williams denied a winner vs. Spurs?
Nottingham Forest 0-0 Tottenham (Sep. 5)
Referee: Craig Pawson

VAR: Peter Bankes

Time: 67 min

Incident: Possible handball to Forest

What happened: Forest defender Neco Williams thought he had given his team the lead as he bundled it across the Spurs goal line. However, VAR overturned the goal for a handball offense.

VAR decision: VAR checked the referee's call of a goal for Forest and determined that Williams handled the ball immediately before scoring and recommended that the goal be disallowed.

VAR review: This was a difficult review for the VAR, which involved multiple angles and replay speeds to determine if this goal should be allowed to stand.

VAR Bankes would have been uncomfortable with the way Williams bundled the ball into the goal, as there was very high chance that it had struck his arm. However, even if the contact was accidental, the law states that any touch of the arm by the goalscorer immediately before a goal must be disallowed.

The in-goal camera provided the decisive information, as it showed the ball striking the arm of Williams as he threw himself in to try and score, creating a change in trajectory of the ball and resulting in a goal -- VAR recommended to the referee that he should disallow the goal for a handball.

Verdict and insight: Not an easy process for the VAR to review. However, once you see the decisive replays from inside Spurs' goal, it is a straightforward decision for the VAR, as the law dictates the outcome.

With so much debate surrounding the Harry Maguire "handball goal" from last week -- when the ball struck the arm of Maguire before his shot was deflected into the goal off a defender, meaning Maguire was not the actual scorer -- this scenario is far clearer and the correct outcome is reached.

How new standards cost Arsenal a clear penalty
Aston Villa 0-1 Arsenal (Aug. 31)
Referee: Jarred Gillett

VAR: James Bell

Time: 90 + 9 mins

Incident: Possible penalty to Arsenal

What happened: Arsenal's Bruno Guimarães was screaming for a penalty after he was challenged from behind by Villa's Ian Maatsen inside the box. Referee Jarred Gillett waved away the appeals.

VAR decision: VAR checked and cleared the on-field decision of no penalty.

VAR review: VAR James Bell clearly applied the new "high bar" for intervention when he cleared this decision, taking the view that the referee's on-field decision not to award a penalty to Arsenal was not a clear and obvious error. After reviewing the replays, VAR quickly checked and cleared the decision as correct.

Verdict and insight: For me, this was a clear penalty kick that should've been awarded to Arsenal. I was surprised it was not given on-field by match referee Gillett, and equally surprised the VAR did not recommend a pitch-side review.

The decision by Villa's Maatsen to challenge in the nature he did, from behind with a scissor action and no opportunity to play the ball was a poor one. By making contact only with Guimarães and none on the ball, there can be little doubt that it met the threshold for a foul -- and it took place inside the penalty box.

The surprising non-intervention by VAR is a result of the Premier League's desire this season to have less involvement and only very clear errors to be corrected, with a new "higher bar" for interventions to be applied.

It's a positive principle that should result in less time spent re-litigating decisions, yes. However, this was clearly a mistake from the on-field referee not to award a penalty and, in my opinion, this was an intervention that has been missed by the VAR team.

Arsenal winning the game will cover the narrative to some degree, however, if this was a deciding moment that cost Arsenal all three points, the profile of the incident would've been significant.

The high bar will absolutely improve the game and lower the expectations from football that VAR should get involved in everything, however it is so important that clear fouls in the penalty area, like this situation, do not get overlooked when the referee has mis-read a key moment.

Why did Maguire's obvious handball not cancel goal?
Manchester United 5-2 Ipswich Town (Aug. 30)
Referee: Craig Pawson

VAR: Jarred Gillett

Time: 56th minute

Incident: Possible handball in lead-up to Man United's second goal by Harry Maguire

What happened: The ball was cleared out of Ipswich's box toward Maguire, and the ball appeared to strike the arm of Maguire. He brought the ball to his feet and struck the ball toward goal, where it then took a grave deflection from Ipswich defender Jacob Greaves before going into the goal. Following a VAR review, the goal was allowed to stand.

VAR decision and communications: The referee's call of goal for Manchester United was checked and confirmed by VAR, who deemed that Maguire was not the immediate goalscorer after an accidental handball.

VAR: "It's an own goal and the accidental handball is not punishable, so we recommend you award the goal."

VAR review: With the knowledge that the ball had clearly struck the arm of Maguire, the VAR had two key elements to consider:

(1) Was Maguire's shot on target before it struck Greaves and entered the goal? In other words: was Maguire the goalscorer?

(2) Was the handball by Maguire accidental or a punishable as an intentional handball offence?

The answers to both questions could have resulted in a different outcome, but the VAR determined that it was clearly an own goal by Greaves, meaning Maguire was not the scorer, and that the handball incident was accidental. Both details meant the ball striking the arm of Maguire was negated in law, and the VAR recommended to the referee that the goal should be awarded.

Verdict and insight: It's understandable that Ipswich Town will feel hard-done by the decision.

If Maguire had scored the goal, then his handling of the ball in the lead-up would've canceled out the goal. It's only because it took the massive deflection that changed the trajectory of the ball that Maguire's incidental handball did not result in the goal being overturned.

In truth, it was a 50/50 decision that could have fallen the other way if the judgement of VAR was a different one. But the law doesn't allow a goal to be disallowed in this situation if the handball by Maguire was judged as accidental.

The subjective nature of handball in general is a confusing element of the game, and if VAR had judged this as a punishable handball and disallowed the goal, it would certainly have been a credible outcome given the context of the situation in my opinion -- and a more comfortable outcome for football.

However, the judgement by VAR Jared Gillett was not an incorrect one, with Maguire challenging for a bouncing ball and his arms in front of his body, the ball striking his left arm can certainly be deemed as accidental. It was on this occasion, with Man United the benefactor of it in this situation, and Ipswich rightfully feeling hard done by.

Should Liverpool have been bailed out by penalty?
Newcastle United 2-2 Liverpool (Aug. 23)
Referee: Stuart Attwell

VAR: James Bell

Time: 90 + 6 mins

Incident: Penalty awarded to Liverpool for a challenge by Lewis Hall on Victor Muñoz

What happened: Liverpool's Muñoz charged into the Newcastle penalty area late into the game, and Hall made a clumsy challenge bringing the Liverpool player to the ground. Referee Stuart Attwell pointed to the spot for a late penalty for the Reds.

VAR decision and communications: The referee's call of penalty for the challenge by Hall on Muñoz was checked and confirmed by VAR.

The referee: "He doesn't play the ball. He makes clear contact."

VAR: "It's knee into thigh contact. Confirming the on-field decision of penalty."

Verdict: This was a correct decision made by referee Atwell and his assistant, and a decision I felt was clear in real-time.

In this type of situation, with an attacker moving into the penalty area at speed with the ball under control, any challenge by a defender must successfully play the ball or they run a very high risk of committing a foul.

Hall was naïve to make his clumsy challenge in the manner he did, and Muñoz was too clever for the Newcastle defender. This was a clear foul by Hall, and a penalty kick a correct outcome.

While it may feel to Newcastle fans that Liverpool were bailed out and gifted a draw after middling performance, Hall's foul was needless and to blame for Liverpool equalizing.

stories.headline: André Luiz, Taylor Calheira help Sporting KC stun LAFC 3-1 to end long winless streak
stories.summary: André Luiz and Taylor Calheira scored first-half goals and Sporting Kansas City shocked Los Angeles FC with a 3-1 victory on Saturday night that ended a seven-match winless streak.
stories.body:
KANSAS CITY, Kan. -- André Luiz and Taylor Calheira scored first-half goals and Sporting Kansas City shocked Los Angeles FC with a 3-1 victory on Saturday night that ended a seven-match winless streak.

Sporting KC (5-16-3) had lost six of seven matches during a skid that began with a 4-0 loss to LAFC (11-8-7) on the road.

Sporting KC jumped in front in the 18th minute when Luiz used assists from defenders Justin Reynolds and Moisés Mosquera to score his first goal in his third MLS appearance. Reynolds' assist was his second and Mosquera notched his first in his seventh league appearance.

Calheira, a first-year forward, scored unassisted in the 31st minute for a 2-0 lead that carried through halftime. Calheira scored for the third time in his eighth start and 16th appearance.

Denis Bouanga cut it to 2-1 two minutes into the second half with his 13th goal this season. Jacob Shaffelburg tied his career high with his fourth assist this season and Son Heung-min collected his 12th - tied with two others for second most in the league.

Sporting KC regained a two-goal lead in the 71st minute on an unassisted goal by Jacob Bartlett - his second netter this season after not scoring last year in his first 30 appearances in the league.

Stefan Cleveland saved six shots for Sporting KC, which began the day with the fewest points in the league.

Hugo Lloris had five saves for LAFC, which began the day in third place in the Western Conference.

Up next Los Angeles: At San Jose Earthquakes on Saturday.

Kansas City: Hosts Philadelphia Union on Saturday.

stories.headline: France tops host Germany to reach FIBA World Cup final
stories.summary: Gabby Williams had 22 points and five rebounds to lead France to the final of the women's FIBA World Cup with a win over host Germany.
stories.body:
BERLIN -- Gabby Williams led France to the final of the women's FIBA World Cup with an 86-64 win over host Germany on Saturday.

Williams scored 22 points and had five rebounds to put France in touching distance of the title after a dogged performance from the host, which refused to give up in front of a partisan crowd at Berlin Arena.

"A tricky game," France coach Jean-Aime Toupane said.

Janelle Salaun had a double-double with 14 points and 11 rebounds, while Marine Johannes, who contributed three 3-pointers among her 13 points, slowed the game down in the final quarter.

"It was really a fight tonight. I think we were ready for that," Johannes said.

It was the first semifinal appearance for both teams since the stage was introduced in 1986.

France will play Spain or the United States, the four-time defending champion and tournament favorite, in Sunday's final. Their semifinal was later Saturday.

There was an air of nervous anticipation around the arena before tipoff as Germany, already further than ever before in its second tournament appearance, would need another major upset to make the final. Germany coach Olaf Lange spoke of "German basketball's best day" after the quarterfinal win over European champion Belgium.

Germany rued 25 turnovers on an evening when French pressure took its toll.

"When you have 25 of them and 10, 12 in my personal opinion were unnecessary or careless, it's very, very difficult to stay in a game against France," Lange said.

Germany, which recovered impressively since losing its opening game to Spain by 30 points, kept France below 90 points for the first time in the tournament and can look forward to the possibility of a bronze medal on Sunday.

"It's our third back-to-back [game] this tournament, which is insane. Honestly, it's crazy in that kind of tournament, a World Cup, to have three back-to-backs," forward Leonie Fiebich said. "We know what to do. We had a really tough game in the first game. We turned around and played really well the next game. So that's our plan, and everything's positive from now on."

stories.headline: Arsenal's Gabriel 'eager' to take another Champions League final penalty: 'If it happens again, I'll be there'
stories.summary: Arsenal defender Gabriel Magalhães has said that he is "eager" for another chance to take a penalty in a Champions League final.
stories.body:
Arsenal defender Gabriel Magalhães has said told ESPN that he is "eager" for another chance to take a penalty in a Champions League final after the heartbreak of missing the crucial spot kick in last season's final against Paris Saint-Germain.

Following an earlier miss from Eberechi Eze in the shootout, Arsenal's hopes of winning their first European trophy rested on the shoulders of the Brazil defender who ultimately sent the ball over the crossbar to crown PSG champions for a second consecutive season.

Gabriel, a stalwart character of the Arsenal defence, told ESPN Brasil that if he was in a similar position again, he would take another penalty.

"I couldn't let a single missed penalty erase everything I'd achieved during the season," he said.

"So, I just thank God for the opportunity to have been there in that moment, it's part of the football.

"But I'm definitely eager for another chance, if it happens again, I'll be there, and if I have to take the penalty, I'll take it. So, that's it."

Arsenal were praised throughout last season's campaign for their solid defence, conceding just seven goals throughout their European campaign.

Gabriel thanked the fans for their continued support despite their European season ending on a sour note.

"I only have to thank the fans," he told ESPN Brasil. "Ever since the final, I've just received a lot of support from them, you know. They were incredible to me, sending very positive messages.

"But like I said, it's part of football. I'm here, and it's not the first time something like this has happened. So, as I said, if there's another penalty for me to take, I'll take it."

- Mikel Arteta 'surprised' by criticism over handling of Gabriel Jesus, Gabriel Martinelli exits

Despite the missed opportunity in the Champions League final, Arsenal did end their 22-year wait for the Premier League title and look as though their form is continuing on into this campaign.

Mikel Arteta's side are yet to drop points this season but face a stiff test when they take on Sunderland at the Stadium of Light on Saturday.

stories.headline: Kimi Antonelli jokes on opening stages of Spanish GP in Madrid: 'Driving like a grandmother'
stories.summary: Kimi Antonelli has said that taking on the brand-new Madring will be like driving like a Grandma in the opening stages of the Spanish Grand Prix on Sunday.
stories.body:
MADRID -- Kimi Antonelli has likened the challenge of the brand-new Madring to driving like a grandmother in the opening stages of Sunday's Spanish Grand Prix.

The Italian youngster was on provisional pole and was looking like the man to beat in qualifying before reigning world champion Lando Norris stunned him to the line by 0.011 seconds.

But the drivers have still been getting to grips with the track and heading into the weekend have referred to the the Madring to being "the most risky" on the Formula 1 calendar and "probably a car killer."

Antonelli joked that drivers will be driving like a grandmother and has warned that the race will be about managing the tyres.

"Yeah, probably it's going to be grandmother driving in the first 10 laps, but let's see," Antonelli said.

"We saw in the long run how steep the degradation can be, especially if you push too early, so let's see. We'll try to see in the moment, maybe tomorrow we're going to race and the degradation is going to be much lower, so we just need to see in the moment.

"Tomorrow is going to be a lot about managing the tyres and not degging [degradation] off, you know, so much as well. We don't really know how the hard tyre is, how resilient it is, so, you know, tomorrow we might have two stops, three stops.

"We'll see, but the key is, yeah, especially in that first stint is to try and manage as much, you know, without giving up too much time trying to manage the tyres."

- McLaren's Lando Norris pips Kimi Antonelli to take thrilling pole for Spanish Grand Prix

- Will Madring live up to reputation as F1 car killer? 'The most risky circuit of the calendar'

- Spanish Grand Prix: Everything you need to know about F1's brand-new Madring

Drivers and teams have no historic data to refer to when it comes to knowing how the car will perform this weekend, but one of the key talking points have been around how difficult it's going to be to overtake.

"I think it's going to be very difficult," Antonelli added. "In practice, I spent two laps behind the Williams trying to painfully get past, but just really difficult, especially because already the deg is quite big, and when you're behind, you start sliding more, and it just makes your life a bit tougher.

"The only thing you can do is try to put pressure on the car in front, try to make them do a mistake or make the deg a bit more, and then you try to play with strategy. But, yeah, especially when you have a very similar pace, it's difficult to make a move."

Antonelli is currently leading the world championship by 66 points adrift from his Mercedes teammate George Russell and will be aiming to take his seventh win of the season.

stories.headline: Dylan Larkin to attend Red Wings camp despite trade request
stories.summary: Longtime captain Dylan Larkin will be at Red Wings training camp despite requesting a trade this offseason. Though Larkin will be in attendance, the team said it will begin the season without a captain.
stories.body:
Longtime Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin will report to training camp in Detroit next week despite his summer trade request.

However the Red Wings announced that they will begin the season without a captain.

"Over the past couple of weeks, Red Wings leadership and I have had several in-depth discussions. I've appreciated those candid conversations, and I will be at training camp with my teammates," Larkin said in a statement. "When new leadership is in place, we'll talk further about the direction of the team. We will keep those conversations private, and I will keep my focus on the season ahead and on the guys in that room."

In July, shortly after Larkin's trade request became public, the Red Wings announced that Steve Yzerman would no longer be the team's general manager. Yzerman, a franchise legend and Hall of Famer, had been GM since 2019. Detroit entered a rebuild in that time and hasn't made the playoffs in 10 years.

In a statement, the Red Wings said they "look forward to seeing Dylan and his teammates at Little Caesars for the start of training camp," which begins Sept. 17.

"Any further discussions or decisions regarding this topic will be made once new hockey operations leadership is in place," the team said.

The Red Wings have hired a search firm, which has been conducting interviews for a new general manager.

Larkin, 30, grew up in nearby Waterford, Michigan, and played at the University of Michigan. He was selected by his hometown team in the first round of the 2014 NHL draft.

He debuted in the 2015-16 season for the Red Wings, and the team made the playoffs in his rookie season -- the final year of the franchise's NHL-record 25-year playoff streak. Detroit lost to Tampa Bay in five games in the first round and hasn't returned since.

Larkin was a key member of the 2026 U.S. men's Olympic team that won its first gold medal since 1980. He was especially important defensively and on special teams, part of a penalty killing unit that went a flawless 18-for-18 in Milan.

The Minnesota Wild -- led by Bill Guerin, also the general manager of Team USA -- have tried to acquire Larkin, according to sources. However the sides have been at a stalemate this summer, especially as Detroit's GM seat is vacant.

Larkin had been Detroit's captain since 2021. He ranks 10th in franchise history in both goals (276) and points (643).

The Red Wings' offseason has been defined by uncertainty. That led in part to the free agent departure of Patrick Kane, who returned to the Chicago Blackhawks. Another key piece of business that's unresolved: ascending star defenseman Simon Edvinsson is due for a contract extension.

stories.headline: Cherry-Evans struggles to deliver as Roosters fall
stories.summary: Daly Cherry-Evans is smart enough to know that the success of his late-career move to the Sydney Roosters will be defined by whether he finishes this year with a premiership or not.
stories.body:
Daly Cherry-Evans is smart enough to know that the success of his late-career move to the Sydney Roosters will be defined by whether he finishes this year with a premiership or not.

Cherry-Evans is 37 and will depart to Super League club Hull FC at the end of the season after his exit from Manly to sign a one-year deal with the Roosters.

The reason the Roosters went so hard to lure the veteran halfback out of the Sea Eagles was his experience in big games such as Sunday's qualifying final.

No player has kicked more field goals in NRL history than Cherry-Evans.

But when push came to shove in the dying moments of Sunday's loss to Penrith at CommBank Stadium, Cherry-Evans couldn't help the Roosters over the line.

After Nathan Cleary slotted a 72nd minute one pointer to edge the Panthers ahead 13-12, Cherry-Evans shanked one effort then aborted a 40m attempt under pressure, as Penrith went on to win 19-12.

Cherry-Evans won a premiership in his first year in the NRL and has spoken of a desire to finish his career in Australia with a second.

If that is to come to fruition, the experienced playmaker is going to have to conjure something special to help the Roosters to the grand final.

Trent Robinson's men play Cronulla next week for the chance to face the Dolphins in a preliminary final.

Cherry-Evans has spent all season working alongside Sam Walker in the halves.

But when his partner went down with an ankle injury two weeks out from the end of the regular season, he was thrust into a new-look combination with Hugo Savala.

Robinson neglected the chance to give the pair time to bed in during their final-round loss to South Sydney.

On Sunday, Cherry-Evans performed the majority of the kicking as he and Savala prodded and probed at an otherwise resolute Penrith defence.

The Roosters only scored two tries. Rob Toia crashed over first after Cherry-Evans and James Tedesco combined in the 20th minute, then Mark Nawaqanitawase produced another freakish solo try with a juggling intercept.

But after that, Easts couldn't find a way through.

Cleary was sinbinned on the stroke of halftime for taking out Savala's legs when the Roosters man kicked the ball away.

But the Roosters were unable to make their advantage count after the break and Cleary came back to bite them, putting his side 80 minutes from the grand final.

Cherry-Evans faces a longer path to get to that point and must deliver in the clutch moments to vindicate his Roosters move.
